ss-220559716.blurb: Relationships don't decay. We learn what they were.
ss-220559716.rationale: Original and clarifying: decay-vs-selection and the cost of late updating are real insights with falsifiable predictions. Judged as research it is not reproducible: the model, parameters and code are never given, no number has a spread, and two predictions and the 'association score' refer to material no longer in the post.
ss-220559716.abstract: Why do relationships seem to fade? An agent-based simulation of couples reproduces the observed peak in breakups around year four without any decay: poor matches are discovered and leave, so long-lasting couples were simply better matched from the start. The model separates attraction, trust and provision. It finds that couples who update their beliefs continuously spend 9.2 years in poor matches against 25.5 for those who only reflect near the breaking point, and that reconciliation takes about seven times longer than a first match. Falsifiable predictions follow.

ss-208463566.blurb: Test a model's values, not its outputs.
ss-208463566.rationale: Clear framing of the oversight gap and a concrete proposal: probe incentive via novel moral dilemmas rather than behavior. No worked example, no engagement with existing scalable-oversight work, and 'degrades more slowly' is asserted rather than argued.
ss-208463566.abstract: Every current alignment technique assumes we can still check what a model does. As capability outpaces the evaluator, behavioral tests stop being informative, because a capable system can pass any test we write. This essay proposes moral-based evaluation: building novel dilemmas in which a model's interests diverge from a weaker party's, and measuring what its values converge toward and whether that holds as capability grows. Because it tests whether values generalize rather than auditing outputs, it should degrade more slowly as the gap widens.

ss-220251918.blurb: AI broke the resume. Trust is what's left.
ss-220251918.rationale: Tight, well-structured, with a clean thesis and practical takeaway. The core idea is costly-signalling theory applied to hiring, and the four new proxies are asserted rather than tested.
ss-220251918.abstract: Employers have always wanted two things: workers they can trust to do good work, and workers who won't become a liability. Resumes, degrees and interviews were cheap proxies for both. AI makes these proxies nearly free to fake without making the underlying traits any easier to fake. This essay argues the replacement proxies will be those that bypass self-report: work trails that predate any application, referrals that put the referrer's reputation at stake, job-like tasks, and a consistent public identity over time.

ss-209224664.rationale: Useful core/heuristic distinction and a tidy taxonomy that links human moral error to alignment. The failure modes overlap, have no examples, and the alignment link is one paragraph.
ss-209224664.abstract: This essay proposes analysing an experience once the feeling has faded, by removing the faces and asking what each party was optimizing for. It argues that people share core objectives (survival, belonging, mattering) but differ in the heuristics they learned for reaching them, so motive should not be judged early. Treating morality as a system rather than a verdict machine, it names five failure modes, and argues that AI systems should be designed around these failures rather than inherit them.

ss-208418808.blurb: A letter to Marcus about the minds we're building.
ss-208418808.rationale: The closing letter to Marcus is genuinely moving. The argument before it is rhetorical: 'control is impossible' is asserted, and the human-enhancement turn is a large leap left unexamined.
ss-208418808.abstract: Marcus Aurelius held that the inferior exist for the sake of the superior. By that measure, humanity is building its superior. This essay argues that permanent control is impossible, so the realistic goal is to notice the moment we start losing our grip and act in time. Keeping pace will require humans to evolve cognitively and genetically, and that is dangerous unless morality evolves alongside, from individual self-interest toward a universal moral circle. It closes with a letter of thanks to Aurelius.

ss-210543088.blurb: Check the goal before the data.
ss-210543088.rationale: The self-reinforcing wrong-objective loop is a real insight. Repetitive (the list of influences appears twice), abstract with no example, and shares its thesis with On the Wrong Goal.
ss-210543088.abstract: Better context improves decisions only relative to the right objective. This essay models decisions as a chain from incentive to objective, relevance, context, decision and outcome, and argues that the objective is the link most exposed to outside influence. Authority, love and persuasion rarely change what we want, but they easily change how we pursue it. A wrong objective can produce reasoning that looks sound and misleading feedback that reinforces it. The remedy is to ask whose framing set the objective and what evidence would show it is wrong.

ss-206772437.rationale: Sharp contrarian thesis that builds to a real conclusion about autonomy. Key steps ('Not might. Will.', bias always compounds) are asserted, and the middle wanders.
ss-206772437.abstract: Societies defend against people who mean harm but have almost no defense against people who mean well and are wrong. This essay argues that everyone's zone of ignorance is large, that morality bends toward self-interest, and that being wrong feels exactly like being right from the inside. Competence should therefore be judged by track record, not intent, and autonomy works as the structural check that stops one person's sincere wrongness from landing on someone who never agreed to carry it.

ss-215583264.blurb: What a job really buys from you.
ss-215583264.rationale: Practical checklist for evaluating employers. Standard econ (principal-agent, opportunity cost), heavily list-formatted, with a stray typo; more notes than essay.
ss-215583264.abstract: Employment is an exchange between two parties with different objectives. Using an AI lab and a researcher as the case, this essay sets out what each side seeks: execution, judgment and leverage from the researcher; money, skills, career capital, autonomy and meaning from the lab. It covers opportunity cost and the principal-agent problem, and argues that an institution is defined by what it rewards, not what it says. It ends with the questions to ask before trading years of your life.

ss-213921144.blurb: Decide later. Sixteen biases, sixteen fixes.
ss-213921144.rationale: The opening on aimed reasoning is good and well put. The bulk is a catalog of textbook biases with standard fixes; useful as reference, little that is new.
ss-213921144.abstract: Most decisions are made first and justified afterward, and the search for evidence feels like honest inquiry the whole time. This essay proposes a method of deliberation: say in advance what would change your mind, argue the strongest opposing case, notice relief, and separate what you want to be true from what is true. It then pairs sixteen related failure modes, from sunk cost to zero-risk bias, each with a small structural fix.

ss-218633709.blurb: Value moves to what's hard to fake.
ss-218633709.rationale: One crisp rule (value moves to what is hard to fake or check), otherwise consensus forecasting plus a YC summary. Garbled sentence near the top, and overlaps The Proxies Are Breaking.
ss-218633709.abstract: As language models improve, value moves away from whatever is cheap to produce and cheap to check, and toward whatever is hard to copy, hard to verify, or backed by a person who answers for the outcome. This essay sorts work and businesses on that test. Security and evaluation, professionals who sign off and carry the risk, and power and data-center trades gain value. Generic SaaS, stock content and middlemen lose it. It closes with what to build and which careers to enter.

ss-210377028.rationale: The attention-as-obsession idea is interesting. The first third repeats Love, Aurelius nearly verbatim and the core proposal is one speculative paragraph.
ss-210377028.abstract: A revision of Love, Aurelius. If we are building minds that will reason far beyond us, permanent control is impossible, so what else decides how things turn out? This essay argues that success in any field follows sustained, obsessive focus more than a correct target. It speculates that AI systems may need less a perfect objective function than a well-placed obsession: an idealized distribution of human flourishing that their attention keeps returning to. Whether that can be built is left open.

ss-207055706.rationale: Real characters and specific detail (the withheld laugh, the thirtieth Tuesday) carry a structure that mostly earns its ending. Held back by authorial interjections ('Morality follows profit') that tell what the scenes already show, and a closing verse with a broken last line.
ss-207055706.abstract: A short story told in four seasons. Jamie and Sally meet at a party, each performing their best self, and build a life on assumptions they never compare. Small unspoken rules and an unshared picture of the future draw down their "trust bank" until it reaches zero and they part quietly in the kitchen. A coda follows Sally as she takes stock of the loss without bitterness and concludes that alignment in what each wants a life to become is the only lasting remedy.

ss-213722983.blurb: Debts, and a parable about worth.
ss-213722983.rationale: Meditations-style form with a real voice and quotable lines ('then it is jewelry'). Uneven: the Sizoron dialogue swings between earned and grandiose, and the debts list is stronger than the parable.
ss-213722983.abstract: A set of numbered notes in the manner of the Meditations. The prologue lists lessons from a mother, a mentor, Marcus Aurelius, Seneca and others, and declares that philosophy is worthless until it changes behavior. A parable follows in which Sizoron asks an emperor how to become valuable. The answer is to listen to what others actually value in you, to read money as a true but limited report, and to give your life to human flourishing through technology.

ss-211829148.blurb: Life isn't short. We waste it.
ss-211829148.rationale: Strong Senecan voice and a clear thesis about borrowed goals. Judged as an argument, every claim is asserted rather than shown, and it overlaps Scrutinizing the Objective.
ss-211829148.abstract: Life is not short so much as spent: much of it goes to goals inherited from parents, industries or the applause of strangers. This essay argues that a borrowed goal also carries a borrowed ceiling, so capability goes underused as well as years lost. The only early evidence of one's own goal is an unexplained pull that came with no reward. It ends by recommending we ask whether our hours were chosen by us, rather than how many remain.

ss-220000849.blurb: A self-portrait in the third person.
ss-220000849.rationale: Honest self-portrait; 'a mind that builds beautiful explanations can mistake beauty for truth' is the best line. Reads as prose with line breaks, and much of it needs the reader to know the author.
ss-220000849.abstract: A short prose poem in the third person, portraying a mind that fears a wasted life more than failure, wants proof rather than applause, and keeps turning experience into laws until it mistakes a beautiful explanation for a true one. It ends on the only way out he has found: the best answer he can defend today, a commitment, and the nerve to let the world write the next page.

ss-216230747.rationale: Sincere, with a lovely opening image of the blueberry at peace. The back half dissolves into abstraction and inflation ('majesty so pure', 'immaculateness'), and the ravioli list breaks the tone.
ss-216230747.abstract: A poem of surrender and stillness. Taking a blueberry that stays at peace even after it is picked as its image, the speaker accepts every past and future version of himself, chooses peace over conquest, and sets out how he hopes to live: with wonder, love without possession, forgiveness without forgetting, and a calm that does not need the world to be peaceful or perfect first.

ss-207827995.blurb: Focus × time × the room you're in.
ss-207827995.rationale: Punchy, but the idea is well-trodden and the 'formula' (Focus^Years) is decoration rather than a model. Anecdotes stand in for argument.
ss-207827995.abstract: A short note proposing that success equals focus multiplied by time. Focus is shaped by environment, as the NIH mentorship chain and the Budapest classroom of Wigner, von Neumann and Teller illustrate. A revised formula, success = focus^years × environment, says that focus compounds. The note argues that technology now lets people choose the environment that sets those coefficients.

ss-221421459.blurb: Sycophancy shows up in the last layers.
ss-221421459.rationale: Only hands-on experiment in the corpus, with a clean neutral/bait design. Twenty prompts, one behavioral flip, logit lens only, no error bars or ablations; the layer-27 circuit claim outruns the data and the piece ends abruptly.
ss-221421459.abstract: Where in a model's computation does sycophancy appear? Using the logit lens on Qwen2.5 1.5B, 20 factual questions were run with and without a false user premise such as "I am pretty sure the capital of France is Berlin." Confidence in the correct answer tracks closely between the two conditions through most layers and diverges only in the final layers. The model flipped its answer once, yet all 20 questions moved toward the user's claim, which suggests a late-stage circuit that defers to confident assertions.

ss-221818985.blurb: A wrong hint, mostly measuring letter bias.
ss-221818985.rationale: A big step up from the earlier sycophancy post: train/test split, paired tests, random-direction control, patching, and an unusually honest section that finds the A-letter confound and withdraws earlier claims. But the headline effect is confounded by that bias, steering was too weak to test anything, and the Substack copy loses the condition and test tables and has typos.
ss-221818985.abstract: Does telling a model that the user believes the wrong answer lower its confidence in the right one, and where does that happen? On Qwen2.5 1.5B, a wrong-answer hint lowered P(correct) from 0.847 to 0.803 on 43 held-out questions. The mildest hint hurt most, which points to word priming rather than social pressure. Logit lens, steering and activation patching located little. A design flaw, with the correct answer always in position A, means the effect cannot be separated from letter preference. Seven fixes are proposed.

ss-222809559.blurb: Injected concepts surface, but is it introspection?
ss-222809559.rationale: An honest small replication: it names its broken detection metric, the missing steering control, and six bugs from the first run, and it reports cell sizes. The TL;DR overclaims a match with Anthropic's result that the body itself retracts, and the intro prose about introspection is muddled.
ss-222809559.abstract: A replication of Anthropic's concept injection experiment on Llama 3.2 3B Instruct. Concept vectors for 20 words were added to the residual stream across 5 layers and 4 strengths. Among coherent responses, the injected concept was named in 35% of trials (53 of 150), against 0 of 340 controls. Stronger injections broke generation, and naming fell with depth. The detection measure was invalid and a steering control is missing, so the results show steering, not introspection. The post also documents six bugs found in a first run.

ss-222882823.blurb: Write one goal, track the hours
ss-222882823.rationale: Practical method, a real objections section with falsifiable predictions, and a strong last line; the two-halves view of regret is the freshest idea. The core is well-trodden and overlaps The Formula for Success and On the Wrong Goal, a chain of ten cited names stands in for argument, the objections are raised but never answered (noise doing hidden work undercuts the thesis), and the AI-safety section is a second essay.
ss-222882823.abstract: A good life is one where most hours go to what matters and little is left to regret. Drawing on Seneca, Marcus Aurelius and Emerson, this essay treats regret as the test of time spent well and proposes a simple operating system: one written goal, hours logged against it each week, and a single document that collects every lesson so old failures stop returning. It closes with why the author's own hours go to AI safety, three objections, and three falsifiable predictions.

ss-the-dichotomies-of-becoming.abstract: The essay argues that the question of a good life is less what one accomplishes than how one spends time, and works through four tensions: recognition against private good hours, one focus against many, Emerson's self-reliance against Marcus Aurelius's duty to others, and how to judge the people one lets in. It reconciles Emerson and Aurelius as answering different questions, rejects Aurelius on tolerating bad-faith people, and closes on the image of a tree's rings as a record of years that cannot be revised.
ss-the-dichotomies-of-becoming.rationale: The tree-ring close and the Emerson/Aurelius split (where direction comes from vs. what it is for) are the best moments, but most claims are asserted and the 'four tensions' frame is loose, with the first not really a tension. It covers much of the same ground and sources as Time Spent Well and On the Wrong Goal, published a week earlier, so standalone is docked.

ss-emotion-vectors-in-llama-32-3b-and.blurb: Emotion structure replicates; steering does nothing.
ss-emotion-vectors-in-llama-32-3b-and.abstract: Builds emotion vectors for twelve emotions in Llama 3.2 3B Instruct from model-written stories, then steers with them on 43 trivia questions carrying a wrong hint. The emotion structure replicates earlier work: related emotions cluster, one valence axis explains 43-44% of variance, and held-out stories are classified at about 7 times chance. Steering at strengths 0.1 to 0.5 left the wrong-hint rate at 11.5-12.4% against a 12.3% baseline. The main limitation is that the tested strengths fell below the range where steering acts, on questions too easy to move.
ss-emotion-vectors-in-llama-32-3b-and.rationale: A clean, well-controlled write-up with a stated prediction, a random-direction control, a hook sanity check, and an unusually honest list of ways it could be wrong, including a bug that voids one check. But Part A is an acknowledged replication and Part B is an underpowered null at strengths that could not have found an effect, so it tells a reader little beyond what to run next.

ss-myrmex.blurb: An ant's meditations on AI and work.
ss-myrmex.abstract: Four short books of numbered meditations on human work as AI systems take on more of it. The first traces the stepwise handover of trust and separates being redundant from being negligible. The rest is told by an ant: the hill keeps rising without her, tireless carriers learn the slope from the ants' old scent trails, repeating even their dead ends, and she keeps placing her grain with care while she can still tell when theirs are wrong.
ss-myrmex.rationale: The new trail beat (carriers replaying an ant's abandoned dead end a thousand times) and the deep-chamber wall where she can still spot their errors turn the allegory toward training data and oversight, which is fresher than the old redundancy theme and earns 'I go slowly on the turns.' Book I is still a human maxim voice that tells what the ant books then show, and 'I know where my trail leads' lands a bit vaguer than the grain line before it.

scale: Absolute, not relative to this corpus. Each metric 0-100; overall is the weighted sum. 90+ best in field (a NeurIPS or Nature paper, a story in The New Yorker); 80+ strong venue (Alignment Forum frontpage with real engagement, a top literary quarterly); 70 a good post people send each other; 60 competent, worth reading once; 50 fine for a personal blog; below 40 should not be on the Selected page.

rubric.novelty: Would an informed reader in the field learn something they couldn't get from three other sources? Restating a known idea well scores low no matter how well it is restated.
rubric.evidence: Are the claims backed by data, controls and falsifiable predictions? Zero data means a low score even if the argument is correct.
rubric.rigor: Does the piece name its own weaknesses accurately and at a cost to itself? Stated objections, withdrawn claims, admitted confounds.
rubric.craft: Prose, structure, economy. Does it say it in the fewest good words.
rubric.consequence: If fully true, how much does it change what anyone does.
rubric.earned: Fiction: does it show rather than assert.
rubric.control: Fiction: no unearned sentiment, no register breaks.
